title: Reading a staged heating profile: fluid core, wall and ceiling along the tube, then across the wall
summary: Axial temperature profiles show what the fluid and the wall are doing stage by stage along a heated tube; the radial profile shows where the temperature drop sits across the wall and the fluid film. Together they answer one question: does the wall stay under its ceiling while the fluid goes from liquid to superheated vapour?

media.alt: Temperature in degrees C against axial position in mm for an 8 mm OD by 1.0 mm wall tube at mass flux 2 kg per m2 s and strain rate 48 per s. Four zones are labelled A Preheat, B Boil, M Mist and S Superheat. The green fluid-core curve rises from 25 to 60 C, then to 120 C, stays at 120 C through the mist zone and rises to 150 C at the outlet. The blue inner-wall curve rises to a 180 C ceiling, drops sharply at zone boundaries, sits on the ceiling through the mist zone, then rises from 150 to 180 C in the superheat zone.

source.note: Group explainer for the tube-sizing figures: the 14-tube length comparison, three axial profiles at 20, 48 and 70 per s, and the radial profile at 48 per s. The figures' own titles carry an internal version tag ('v6 MtG'); this explainer does not use it.

read_the_figure.question: Along the tube, in which stage is the fluid, how hot is the wall relative to its 180 C ceiling, and how long must the tube be for each strain rate and tube choice?
read_the_figure.axes: Axial figures (04 to 06): x is axial position in mm, y is temperature in degrees C from about 20 to 200. Shaded bands mark four stages A Preheat, B Boil, M Mist, S Superheat. Dotted horizontal lines mark the bubble point T_bub = 60 C and dew point T_dew = 120 C; the dashed grey line is the wall ceiling at 180 C. Radial figure (07): x is radius from 0 to about 4 mm, one panel per zone, y is temperature. Figure 03: left, thermal length in mm against strain rate in 1/s for all feasible tubes (legend of 14 tube types); right, a bar chart of the same length at 70 per s.
look_at: Green is the fluid core, blue the inner wall, orange the outer wall, red the sheath (outer surface). Where the wall and fluid lines are far apart, heat is being driven through a thick film.
Stage boundaries (thin vertical lines): the blue wall curve drops sharply at the A to B boundary and again at M to S. These are discontinuities of the staged calculation, not physical jumps.
The mist stage is flat on both curves: fluid core held at 120 C (the dew point) and wall on the 180 C ceiling. That is where the largest share of length is spent.

Across the three strain rates the stage structure is the same and the tube gets longer: about 311 mm at 20 per s (G = 1 kg/m2 s), 727 mm at 48 per s (G = 2) and 945 mm at 70 per s (G = 4), read off the end of each axis.

Figure 03: all tubes rise roughly linearly with strain rate, and one light-blue curve (8 mm OD by 1.5 mm wall) turns downwards above about 53 per s. In the bar chart it is the short bar, about 700 mm against 1000 to 1200 mm for the others.
read_the_figure.proves: That the staged design keeps the inner wall at or below its 180 C ceiling over the stated flow range while the fluid is taken from 25 C to a 150 C outlet. It does not prove the model is right: no measurements are shown.
if_wrong: A wall curve crossing the dashed ceiling: the design is infeasible at that flow.
A fluid core that never reaches T_dew before the end of the tube: the vaporisation is incomplete and the outlet is a two-phase mixture.

Sharp wall-temperature jumps at stage boundaries that are large compared with the surrounding changes: the stage model is being forced to switch its wall condition, and the real wall would vary smoothly.
A curve that decreases with flow in figure 03 (the 1.5 mm wall line) is a feasibility or regime switch in the model rather than a physical improvement.
must_check: The stage boundaries are drawn and the stage names are legible (here the labels A Preheat and B Boil overlap at the top).
Both the flow rate and the strain rate are stated in each title.
That the same tube, flow and ceiling are used in all panels of a comparison.
The length definition in figure 03 and the profile end positions agree, or the difference is explained.
Which fluid and which blend the profile is for; here T_bub and T_dew imply a mixture with a wide boiling range.
as_drawn: Values are read off the figures by eye, about 10 percent. Axial figure 05: fluid core 25 C at the inlet, 60 C at the end of preheat (about 27 mm), 120 C at the end of boil (about 77 mm), constant 120 C through the mist zone to about 303 mm, then 150 C at the outlet at about 727 mm. The inner wall reaches the 180 C ceiling at the end of the preheat zone, falls to about 91 C at the zone boundary, rises to about 140 C at the end of the boil zone, then sits at 180 C through the mist zone, falls to 150 C and climbs to 180 C at the outlet.

Stage lengths from the three axial plots (mm): 04: preheat about 11, boil to 39, mist to 134, outlet 311; 05: 27, 77, 303, 727; 06: 40, 103, 378, 945. The mist and superheat stages take the bulk of the length in every case.
Length against flow: 945 / 311 = 3.0 for a fourfold increase in mass flux (G from 1 to 4), so length grows more slowly than the flow.

Radial figure 07 at 48 per s (printed labels): zone A, bulk 60 C, wall 180 C, sheath 182 C; zone B, bulk 117 C, wall 142 C, sheath 148 C; zone M, bulk 120 C, wall and sheath about 180 C; zone S, bulk 150 C, wall and sheath about 180 C. The fluid-side temperature drop is 120 K, 25 K, 60 K and 30 K, against drops through the 1 mm wall of about 2 K, 6 K, 0.3 K and 0.2 K.

Two consistency points for the owner: the text of the caption for figure 05 says the inner wall tracks the ceiling through the boil zone, but the plot and figure 07 show about 140 C there; and the 8 mm OD by 1.0 mm tube length in figure 03 (about 790 mm at 48 per s and 1000 mm at 70 per s) exceeds the end of the axial profile (727 and 945 mm) by roughly 6 to 8 percent, with no stated margin.

terms.meaning: For a counterflow burner, the velocity gradient of the gas stream near the stagnation plane; here the quantity that sets the required fuel flow and so the length of the vaporiser.
Mass flow per unit flow area.
For a liquid mixture, the temperatures at which boiling starts (T_bub) and finishes (T_dew) at the given pressure.
The four stages the fluid goes through: liquid heated to boiling, liquid boiled off, droplets in vapour evaporated, vapour heated beyond the dew point.
The maximum allowed wall temperature, here 180 C, chosen to avoid cracking or degrading the fuel at the wall.
The tube length needed to deliver the heat duty at the stated flow.
The resistance to heat flow in the thin fluid layer next to the wall, usually larger than the resistance of a thin metal wall.
Steady heat flow through a tube wall, where temperature varies with the logarithm of the radius.

remember: Four stages: heat the liquid, boil it, evaporate the mist, superheat the vapour.
During boiling and mist the fluid temperature is set by the mixture's boiling range; the wall can be much hotter.
The wall must stay under its ceiling; the profile is the evidence.
Heat balance: length is proportional to mass flux times the heat to be added, divided by the wall flux.
In a thin metal wall the temperature drop is small compared with the film drop.

understand.title: Why the wall curve jumps
understand.text: The tube is solved stage by stage, and at each boundary the control logic restarts: the wall target changes from heater-limited to ceiling-limited and back. A discontinuity in the plot marks where the model switches condition, not a sudden wall cooling.

understand.title: Why the mist stage is flat
understand.text: While droplets evaporate, nearly all the heat goes into latent heat, so the fluid core holds at 120 C while the wall sits on the ceiling. The 60 K difference between the lines is the driving force for that stage.

understand.title: Why the lengths differ by tube
understand.text: Figure 03 shows that all tubes need the same order of length at a given strain rate: the spread is about 20 percent at 70 per s. The 8 mm OD by 1.5 mm tube is the one outlier, whose curve turns down at high strain rate: that is a model feature to explain before it is trusted.

steps.title: Energy balance for one stage
steps.note: The heat added to the stream in a stage equals the wall flux times the heated area. For fixed Delta h and q'' the length is proportional to the mass flux G, in line with the rising curves in figure 03.

steps.title: Heat flux across the film
steps.note: Newton's law of cooling for the fluid side, with film coefficient h and fluid bulk temperature T_f.

steps.title: Steady conduction through a tube wall
steps.note: Heat per unit length through a cylinder of conductivity k. With r_i = 3 mm and r_o = 4 mm, ln(4/3) = 0.288.

steps.title: Ratio of the two resistances
steps.note: The same heat flows through both, so the temperature drops are in proportion to the resistances. Read the drops off figure 07: zone A is 2 K over 120 K, about 0.02; zone B is 6 K over 25 K, about 0.24.

steps.title: The film coefficient from the profile
steps.note: Eliminate the flux between the two laws. This needs the wall conductivity, which the figures do not give; the worked example assumes a typical stainless-steel value.

steps.title: Laminar reference
steps.note: For fully developed laminar flow in a round tube the Nusselt number is a constant, 3.66 for constant wall temperature and 4.36 for constant flux. The curved, parabola-like fluid profiles in zones A, M and S of figure 07 are what laminar conduction looks like.

worked.title: Film coefficient in the preheat zone from the radial profile
worked.problem: Zone A of figure 07: bulk 60 C, inner wall 180 C, sheath 182 C, r_i = 3 mm, r_o = 4 mm. Assume a wall conductivity of 16 W/(m K) (typical stainless steel; not on the figure). Estimate h and compare with the laminar Nusselt number for a fluid conductivity of 0.5 W/(m K) (also assumed).

solution.text: Temperature drops: wall 2 K, fluid 120 K. Insert in the elimination formula.
Nusselt number with the 6 mm inner diameter.

worked.answer: About 310 W/(m2 K) and Nu about 3.7, close to the laminar value 3.66. With the assumed properties the reading from the plot is consistent with laminar flow; the conclusion depends on the assumed conductivities.

analyze.q: The wall curve drops from about 180 C to about 91 C at the preheat to boil boundary in figure 05. Why is that a modelling artefact and what would the real wall do?
analyze.hint: Heat conduction along the wall smooths such steps over a few diameters.

analyze.q: Length grows from 311 to 945 mm when G grows fourfold. Why not fourfold?
analyze.hint: Think about q'' and the stage lengths, and note that strain rate also changes.

analyze.q: In figure 07 the temperature drop in the fluid is several tens of kelvin while the wall drop is a few kelvin or less. What does that say about which resistance to improve to shorten the tube?

evaluate.q: The 8 mm OD by 1.5 mm tube length in figure 03 drops at high strain rate. Would you pick it because it is shortest at 70 per s?
evaluate.hint: Is the model result physical or a switch?

evaluate.q: The three axial profiles share the same shape. Does that show the design is valid across the envelope, or only that the model behaves the same way?

create: Annotate figure 05 with the fraction of total length taken by each stage, and decide whether the mist stage is the best place to spend a second heater zone.
Design an experiment with three thermocouples that tests the predicted stage boundaries at the 48 per s condition, and say what reading would falsify the model.

checks.q: Why is the fluid-core temperature flat during the mist stage?
checks.answer: The heat goes into latent heat of evaporation of the droplets, so the core stays at the dew point (here 120 C) while the wall stays on the ceiling.

checks.q: Axial lengths are 311 mm at G = 1 and 945 mm at G = 4. What is the length ratio?
checks.answer: 945 / 311 = 3.0, less than the fourfold change in G.

checks.q: In zone A the fluid-side drop is 120 K and the wall drop 2 K. Which resistance dominates?
checks.hint: The resistances are in proportion to the drops.
checks.answer: The fluid film: it carries 60 times the temperature drop of the wall for the same heat flow.

checks.q: The wall curve jumps at stage boundaries. How should this affect how you use the profile?
checks.answer: Treat the stage averages and the ceiling margin as the result, not the jump positions; a smooth wall solution would be needed to read local values.

checks.q: What extra curve would make the axial figure answer the vapour-quality question?
checks.hint: Add an output that tracks the phase.
checks.answer: A vapour mass-fraction (quality) curve against position, from 0 at T_bub to 1 at T_dew, or a shaded two-phase region.
